title: What's the Difference Between an Architect and a Designer?
excerpt: People often use the words "architect" and "designer" interchangeably, but they're not the same thing. Here's what you need to know before hiring someone for your Westchester home project.
content:
If you're planning a home renovation in Westchester NY, you've probably heard both terms thrown around. Someone calls themselves a designer. Someone else is an architect. They might seem like they do the same work, but there's an important difference, and it matters for your project.

The main distinction comes down to licensing and legal responsibility. A licensed architect in New York has met specific educational requirements, passed rigorous exams, and carries professional liability insurance. When you hire a licensed architect, you're getting someone who can stamp and sign off on construction documents. That seal means something in the eyes of building departments and local inspectors. A designer, by contrast, creates aesthetically pleasing spaces but doesn't carry that same legal authority or training.

Why Licensing Matters

Building departments across Westchester take licensing seriously. Whether you're working with a contractor in Westchester or filing plans in Scarsdale, Bronxville, or Mamaroneck, municipal officials need to know that someone qualified has reviewed the structural and safety aspects of your project. A licensed architect has studied building codes, structural systems, and how buildings actually work. Designers excel at making spaces beautiful, but they typically don't have the technical training to certify that a second-story addition won't compromise your home's integrity.

This becomes critical during the permitting phase. When you pull permits for home additions in Westchester, inspectors want an architect's signature on certain documents. Not every project requires this, but it depends on scope and local requirements. A residential architect in Scarsdale knows which projects need that formal stamp and which ones don't.

The Design-Build Advantage

Here's where things get interesting. At House Architecture and Construction, our principal is both a licensed architect and a general contractor. That's not common. Most firms are one or the other. Silvio M. Luca runs every project personally, which means your architect is also your builder. He oversees everything from initial concept through final walkthrough.

This matters when you're planning a kitchen remodel in Pelham, a primary suite addition in Rye, or a complete open-concept conversion in Tarrytown. When one person holds both licenses, there's no translation layer between the design drawings and what actually gets built. The architect isn't handing plans to someone else and hoping they understand the vision. He's there making sure it happens right.

What Kind of Help Do You Actually Need?

Not every project requires a licensed architect. A small bathroom renovation in White Plains might be handled perfectly well by a skilled designer and contractor working together. But if you're doing a custom home in Westchester County, adding a second story in Harrison, or tackling a historic restoration in Hastings-on-Hudson, having an architect involved protects you and ensures compliance with local codes.
